newsitem.title: POLAND: FEATURE - British army mounts historic manouevres in Poland.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - British army mounts historic manouevres in Poland.

text.p: DRAWSKO POMORSKIE TRAINING AREA, Poland, Sept 6 - Five years ago the sight of 12 British heavy battle tanks roaring across the Polish plains would have been an early sign that World War Three had started.
But their presence in Poland today reflects Britain's urgent need for areas to manoeuvre in to keep its armed forces on their toes in the wake of the Cold War.

As Germany started closing its training grounds for environmental reasons, British eyes focused on the huge Drawsko Pomorskie region of northwest Poland where elite Soviet forces once practised their plans for invading Europe.
For the Poles, the chance to help Britain brings both much-needed hard cash as well as a chance to improve ties at a time when it is seeking support for its bid to join NATO.

So from August 30 until September 20 some 3,500 men and 1,250 armoured vehicles are mounting "Operation Ulan Eagle", the first time a British brigade has practised for high intensity warfare since the 1991 Gulf War.

British commanders are delighted with Drawsko Pomorskie -- the largest of several Polish former Warsaw Pact training areas -- saying its 400 square km (155 square miles) offer a greater variety of terrain than many other practise grounds they have seen.

"It's ideal for our purposes. There are large areas of woods, many lakes and many bogs," said Brigadier David Montgomery, commander of the 7th Armoured Brigade, the famed "Desert Rats" who fought with distinction in World War Two and in the Gulf War.
"It's the first time we've trained on such terrain and that makes it very special. We have been genuinely struck by the warmth and the cooperation from the Poles," he told reporters.

Britain also uses huge Canadian training areas which cover 259,000 square km (100,000 square miles), but the expense and logistical problems mean they use borrowed equipment and cannot commit more than 1,200 men at any one time.
In contrast, Drawsko Pomorskie is just 600 km (375 miles) from the Desert Rats' German bases, giving the troops valuable experience of moving their own equipment across Europe.
Ulan Eagle, which simulates full-scale combat rather than peacekeeping, is purely British, although Polish forces are present as observers and engineers will build a bridge.
The British troops clearly revelled in the experience of exploring a totally unknown area.
"It's good to go somewhere new. We knew our old German training grounds so well we didn't need a map," said Major Paddy Allison, leaning against his Challenger main battle tank.
"Here we make the drivers and tank commanders earn their pay. And for us, half the use of the exercise was the deployment here and the return to Germany."
Rather than drawing lines across the Canadian prairies and pretending they represented rivers, British troops in Poland have a wide range of real water obstacles to tackle.

"The manoeuvring areas are brilliant. There's a good mix of open ground, lots of obstacles, some big and some small," said Major Jake Thackray, deputy chief of staff of 7th Army Brigade, his face smeared with camouflage paint.
The British -- who the Poles said had paid $1.5 million to rent the training area -- plan to return next year, by which time their hosts should have improved the facilities.

"We got a bloody good deal for the Polish training ground. If the price had not been reasonable, we would not have trained there," said British Defence Minister Nicholas Soames as he toured the area with his Polish and Ukrainian counterparts.
The British say there is no chance they will abandon the huge training areas in Canada just yet.
"We've invested a fortune in Canada, where we train for a general war. It's the hardest kind of training and is good for campaigns in the Middle East," said Thackray.
"The most important aspect of the Canadian grounds is the freedom of manoeuvre."
A much smaller detachment of British troops is also training in western Ukraine and Soames said Kiev was keen to broaden military cooperation.

"The Ukrainian defence minister wants us to train with tanks and planes. The better we understand each other, the less room there is for misunderstandings," he said, adding that this would give Britain a chance to boost its influence in Kiev.
"Our policy is not linked to being nice to them so we can sell them lots of armoured equipment. They'd rather train with us than with a lot of other people," said Soames.
"The Ukrainians also have very good air-to-ground ranges which would suit our Harrier jets perfectly."

Both Poland and Ukraine are members of NATO's Partnership for Peace Programme, but Kiev is very unhappy about Warsaw becoming a full member of the Alliance because it fears any possibility of Western nuclear weapons being deployed closer to its borders than present.
The three countries announced they had agreed to cooperate more closely in defence matters, but said details had to be worked out.
